topic: automated program repair; fault localization; input robustness
status: cross-era bounded synthesis; shared causal interaction untested
claim: Three APR studies spanning search-based and LLM-based repair indicate that repair outcomes depend on what code/context reaches the repair stage, not only on the repair algorithm. A 2017 GenProg study found fault-space accuracy correlated with repair success and search cost, and selected augmented-test cases reduced patch validations (Math 5: 306 to 28), while another case worsened localization. A 2025 LLM study found repair-relevant prompt context substantially improved four selected models on transformed Defects4J, yet 10/12 tested model/prompt setups remained below original-set performance. A 2026 independent study found all seven models significantly declined on transformed Defects4J bugs solvable in their original form, but newer GitBug-Java did not show significant mean declines for GPT-4o/Claude-3.7; the smaller sample had low power and large bug-level exceptions. Taken together, localization, context and representation are plausible interacting factors in APR performance, but these heterogeneous studies do not demonstrate a common mechanism or directly comparable effect sizes.

locators: §3: two datasets and ten prompt runs per original/transformed bug
§4.1/Table 2: Defects4J declines and GitBug-Java non-significant mean cases

interpretation: This is an opportunity synthesis across different generations and methods, not an effect-size meta-analysis. Search-based fault localization, LLM prompt context and semantics-preserving transformations are different interventions/outcomes. Evidence supports testing their interaction, not presuming it.
falsifiable_question: In a shared APR benchmark, does fault-localization quality or bug-report context moderate the success-rate penalty from natural semantics-preserving code transformations? Does improved localization recover transformed-input performance, or do representation changes independently impair patch generation after controlling for original solvability, project, test strength and inference budget?
primary_outcome: Paired human-verified correct repair rate and test-adequate rate by original/transformed input, localization/context arm and bug; secondary outcomes are time/patches searched, per-transformation effect, and held-out-project performance. Report null and severe individual regressions.
counterevidence_and_caveats: The 2017 study reports concrete cases where better fault-space accuracy reduces search cost and one case where test augmentation worsens localization.
The 2025 study shows repair context helps materially; it does not erase the representation gap for most tested setups.
The 2026 study finds no significant mean drop for two closed models on the newer benchmark, which limits universal claims; limited sample power and per-bug regressions remain.
Studies differ in algorithms, model generations, datasets, correctness criteria, prompts and denominators; their percentages must not be pooled.

2017 study is GenProg/Java/four Defects4J projects and uses developer-changed lines as localization oracle; 2025 transformed variants derive from 438 original Java defects; 2026 large-scale outcome is test adequacy.
NLL is only a familiarity proxy and does not prove training exposure.
Only three studies were cross-read here; no new causal experiment or global novelty search was completed.
suggested_design: Use original and independently collected time-stamped Java bugs, then apply human-validated natural transformations. Cross high/low localization quality with no context, bug report and trigger-test context in matched model runs; hold out projects and tune budgets on validation only. Score hidden tests plus blinded semantic review, repeat seeds/prompts, and report interaction estimates, task-level exceptions and applicability limits.

topic: distributed data systems; scientific imaging; benchmark transfer
status: bounded within-study workload contrast; modern replications needed
claim: A two-workload comparison of SciDB, Myria, Spark, Dask and TensorFlow on neuroscience and astronomy image pipelines shows no single performance ranking that transfers across operation, input scale, node count, memory policy and data conversion. In the tuned end-to-end setup, Dask is at most 14% faster than Spark/Myria in a reported comparison, is 60% slower for one-subject input, and approaches or exceeds peers only as scale amortizes startup costs. At individual operations, a tool may be best for one kernel and much worse for another; SciDB's >10× slower iterative astronomy co-add is explicitly tied to the evaluated release's lack of iterative optimization. The supported implication is conditional system selection and full-pipeline measurement, not that any one engine is generally superior.

sources.title: Comparative Evaluation of Big-Data Systems on Scientific Image Analytics Workloads
locators: §§3–4: two end-to-end neuroscience/astronomy pipelines and five implementations
§5.1: end-to-end scale curves and 16–64-node behavior
§5.2: operation-specific ranking and >10× SciDB iterative co-add result
§5.3: tuning, memory and caching tradeoffs
§§6–8: limits and conclusions

interpretation: The authors compare genuine scientific pipelines, but only two workflows, an older 2016 system snapshot and cloud instance environment. They tuned the implementations; SciDB's iterative result is version/optimization-specific. This is a candidate workload-aware benchmark design, not a current recommendation about engines.
falsifiable_question: Across a version-pinned collection of modern astronomy, neuroscience and at least two additional image pipelines, do operation-level microbenchmarks predict end-to-end engine ranking after controlling data layout, conversion cost, tuning budget, memory pressure and node count? Does an out-of-box ranking differ materially from an expert-tuned ranking?
primary_outcome: End-to-end wall time, peak memory, scaling efficiency and implementation effort per workload, reported alongside operation-level latency, format-conversion time, tuning time and failure rate under fixed data/hardware conditions.
counterevidence_and_caveats: The original comparison shows similar end-to-end performance for Spark and Myria in some conditions and near-linear Myria scaling, rather than one universal winner.
Dask's small-input penalty and later-scale improvement show why a single dataset size can reverse rankings.
An unoptimized SciDB release explains at least one large deficit; the paper itself references prior optimizations that could change it.
Only two scientific workloads and older platform versions were tested; conclusions do not transfer to current systems without rerunning.
Expert tuning means the measurements are not an out-of-box user comparison.
suggested_design: Reimplement each workload on pinned current releases; preregister common hardware, input-size ladder, data formats, correctness checks and equal tuning budgets. Run both expert-tuned and default configurations, repeat runs, cross workload/version folds, and report memory/failure/engineering effort in addition to throughput.

status: within-paper sensitivity plus prior regime-conditional counterevidence; replication needed
claim: UCL reports strong retention/average performance on several supervised continual-learning benchmarks and an eight-task continuous-control sequence, but its own supplement shows results depend jointly on β and initial uncertainty: smaller initial uncertainty can reduce exploration and prevent learning later tasks even when forgetting is controlled. In the separate coreset study audited earlier, memory-selection gains also vary across balanced versus imbalanced streams and its reported β is selected on test performance. These are different algorithms and data regimes, so they do not establish one shared cause; together they motivate evaluating continual-learning methods across stability, new-task acquisition, stream regime and leakage-safe model selection rather than ranking by one average score.

sources.title: Coresets via Bilevel Optimization for Continual Learning and Streaming
locators: §6.3: differing balanced versus imbalanced streaming results
Appendix E: β chosen using best test-set result
§7: scope and stated limitations

interpretation: The UCL article demonstrates good benchmark outcomes under selected settings and explicitly warns through its own supplemental sensitivity that the stability/plasticity controls matter. The coreset study supplies a separate counterexample to universal method rankings and a model-selection concern, not a direct replication. Keep methods, architectures, task orders and validation protocols distinct.
falsifiable_question: Under a preregistered factorial continual-learning study, how do methods trade off old-task retention and new-task learning as task order, task similarity, stream balance and model capacity vary? Are method rankings robust when all hyperparameters are selected on validation streams rather than test outcomes?
primary_outcome: Per-task accuracy/reward before and after each update, forgetting and forward transfer, final and worst-task performance, memory/compute cost, plus hyperparameter-selection protocol; report repeated-seed uncertainty and stream-regime interactions.
counterevidence_and_caveats: UCL reports strong outcomes versus several baselines across multiple image benchmarks and one continuous-control sequence; parameter sensitivity does not negate those results.
UCL CNN experiments report eight random seeds, while some smaller MLP benchmark sections do not state the same repeat count in the main description.
The UCL supplement shows a particular initial-uncertainty setting can impair new-task learning, so high average results do not establish robust taskwise behavior.
The coreset study's balanced/imbalanced and test-selection details come from a different method and cannot be pooled with UCL outcomes.
Only a small number of methods and task families were audited; global novelty is unconfirmed.
suggested_design: Compare regularization, replay and coreset methods under common architectures and update budgets. Cross balanced/imbalanced and stationary/shifted streams, multiple task orders and capacity budgets; tune only on a separate validation stream. Publish per-task curves, failure cases, selection costs and fixed-seed scripts.
